title: Pauri 12, sound: mannai
hookLine: mannai kee gat kahee na jaae
last: ASAGAAH — THE BLIND FIND THE WAY.

cards: Your friend says, get some sleep. You hear it. And you stay up anyway.
Hearing advice and taking it are two different things. Hearing is the first step; something else has to happen for the words to move in. Japji knows this.

teach.b: The new word is mannai. Say it with the n held a moment: MUN-nai.
It comes from the Punjabi verb mannanaa, and that verb is wide: to accept, to agree, to obey, to believe, to trust, to take something to heart.
When a Punjabi mother tells a child, gall mann lai, she means take my word, go along with it. In Japji, mannai means by trusting, by taking the Word to heart.
For the next four stanzas, pauris 12 to 15, line after line begins with it, the way the last four began with suniai.

teach.h: MANNAI KEE GAT KAHEE NA JAAE.
teach.b: Here's the first line of Pauri 12 in the original: mannai kee gat kahee na jaae. Mannai kee, of the one who trusts. Gat, the state, the condition someone is in.

Kahee na jaae, cannot be told. The state of the one who trusts cannot be put into words. Hear the rhythm: mannai kee gat, three quick beats, then kahee na jaae, slowing down, as if the sentence itself runs out of breath.
Tomorrow, what it means. Today is for the sound.
And notice the order Guru Nanak chose: first suniai, listening, then mannai, trusting.
One way Sikh teachers describe the path: you hear the Word, then you take it in, then you live it. A word goes in the ear, then it goes home.

how: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; pauris 12 to 15 each begin with mannai, and the move from suniai, listening, to mannai, trusting, is often taught as steps on one path.

o: by singing, praising it out loud
by trusting, taking the Word to heart

games.q: the sound of Pauri 12 — tap the pairs.
p: the word of the last four stanzas

s: mannai only means to believe an idea
mannanaa is wide: to accept, obey, trust and take to heart.
pauris 12 to 15 all begin with mannai
just as pauris 8 to 11 all began with suniai.
in Japji, listening comes before trusting

games.q: you've just listened to four stanzas about listening. what does Japji do next?
o: starts four stanzas of trusting, mannai.
tells a story about a king.
games.why: pauris 12 to 15 each begin with mannai: the Word that was heard now has to be taken to heart.

practice: Say mannai slowly, five times, each on a full breath out: MUN-nai, hold the n, then let the ending open. Rest in the quiet for a few breaths between each.
If it helps, let the word sit beside one thing you've heard and haven't yet taken to heart.

wordCard.voice: Mannai. By trusting, by taking the Word to heart. It opens line after line of pauris 12 to 15, after four stanzas of listening.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: mannai, by trusting or accepting; from mannanaa, to accept, obey, believe.

carryVoice: Your line: mannai, trusting. For the next four stanzas, it leads the way. Until tomorrow.
